devastated

/DEV-uh-stay-tid/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Devastated means severely damaged or destroyed on a large scale, or overwhelmed by disaster, shock, or grief.

After the tornado, volunteers arrived from three states to help the devastated town rebuild.

Example

Grandpa Ito had tended his bonsai collection for forty years. The August hailstorm shattered the greenhouse in twenty minutes, snapping trunks older than his grandchildren. For days he could hardly speak about it. Seeing him so devastated, the neighbors pooled money for new glass — and saved the three trees that could still be grafted.

Grandpa Ito's greenhouse is physically ruined and he is emotionally crushed by the loss — devastated captures both the destruction and the overwhelming grief.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

crushed: Crushed describes a person flattened by grief or disappointment — a purely emotional blow. Devastated can carry that same emotional weight, but it also describes physical wreckage on a large scale: a devastated town, a devastated coastline. A person is crushed by bad news; a person or a whole coastline can be devastated.

shattered: Shattered pictures a person or thing broken into pieces — one blow, many fragments — and for feelings it means composure completely broken. Devastated points to the aftermath of a heavy blow on the largest scale, physical or emotional. Bad news leaves a fan shattered; a hurricane leaves a coast devastated.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

thriving: healthy, strong, and doing well

untouched: left without any damage

Where it sits · how crushing the blow is

shaken → devastated → annihilated

shaken vs. devastated: Someone shaken is upset but still functioning; someone devastated is overwhelmed by the blow.

annihilated vs. devastated: Annihilated goes beyond devastated — wiped out completely, with nothing left at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-: completely (Latin, intensive)

Root — vast-: empty, laid waste (Latin vastus/vastare)

Suffix — -ated: made into; having been acted upon

Put it together: Devastated builds on Latin vastare, 'to lay waste,' from vastus, 'empty.' The same root gives us vast — originally an emptied, desolate expanse. So a devastated town has literally been made vast: emptied out by destruction. Vest and festive only resemble it by accident.

Use the root in a new word: vast: A vast desert is literally an 'emptied' landscape — Latin vastus, the same root that lets devastated mean laid waste.

Word Choice

everyday and journalistic; strong

Devastated works two ways — a devastated coastline (physically laid waste) or a devastated parent (emotionally overwhelmed); either way it describes the aftermath of a heavy blow, unlike hazardous (another word in this unit), which flags danger before harm has occurred.
